::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
## TL;DR

Spreading crushed basalt on cropland draws down $\text{CO}_2$, but dissolving it also raises soil pH, and soil pH steers the nitrogen cycle. Val Martin and colleagues gave the Community Land Model (CLM5) pH-dependent nitrification and denitrification and a pH-dependent ammonia scheme, then fed it the soil pH changes that a separate weathering model predicts for basalt deployment large enough to remove $2\text{ Gt CO}_2\text{ yr}^{-1}$. Across the five regions studied, agricultural nitrous oxide ($\text{N}_2\text{O}$) falls $19\%$ ($0.42\text{ Tg N yr}^{-1}$) and nitric oxide ($\text{NO}$) $17\%$, while ammonia ($\text{NH}_3$) rises $2\%$; North America changes most, with $\text{N}_2\text{O}$ down $28\%$. Afterwards you should be able to explain why the same pH rise that cuts $\text{N}_2\text{O}$ raises $\text{NH}_3$, and how the weathering and land models were coupled.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## Corrected, October 2026

An earlier version of this page reported a regional results table, a basalt application rate and a "climate bonus" of $12$–$20\%$ that are not in the paper it cited, said the weathering chemistry was computed inside CLM5, and cited two references whose DOIs pointed to unrelated records. The weathering is computed by a separate model coupled to CLM5, and the paper gives no CO$_2$-equivalent benefit. The page and its interactive widget, which was built on the same numbers, have been replaced with what the paper reports[^4].
:::

## How crushed rock removes carbon

Natural silicate weathering is the Earth's long-term thermostat[^1]. Silicate minerals such as forsterite olivine, or the calcium- and magnesium-rich minerals in basalt, react with carbonic acid in soil water:

$$\text{Mg}_2\text{SiO}_4 + 4\,\text{CO}_2 + 4\,\text{H}_2\text{O} \to 2\,\text{Mg}^{2+} + 4\,\text{HCO}_3^- + \text{H}_4\text{SiO}_4$$

The dissolved bicarbonate ($\text{HCO}_3^-$) and the cations that balance it are carried by rivers to the ocean, where the carbon stays for very long periods. Grinding the rock finely and spreading it on fields, where soil acidity, water and roots speed dissolution, is **enhanced rock weathering** (ERW): the same reaction run on a timescale of years rather than geological epochs[^2]<sup>,</sup>[^5].

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    CO2["Atmospheric CO2 in soil water"] --> Rock["Crushed basalt on cropland"]
    Rock --> Diss["Dissolution: Ca2+, Mg2+ and bicarbonate released"]
    Diss --> Ocean["Bicarbonate carried to the ocean"]
    Diss --> pH["H+ consumed: soil pH rises"]
    pH --> Ncycle["Soil nitrogen cycle shifts"]

    class CO2 indigo
    class Rock olive
    class Ocean indigo
    class pH ochre
    classDef indigo fill:#1d4a62,stroke:#c97d62,stroke-width:1.5px,color:#ffffff
    classDef olive fill:#5b6e34,stroke:#c97d62,stroke-width:1.5px,color:#ffffff
    classDef ochre fill:#d69a2e,stroke:#3b1a18,stroke-width:1.5px,color:#3b1a18
```

The reaction consumes hydrogen ions, which is why the same process that removes carbon also raises soil pH. That side effect is the subject of the rest of this module.

## What the pH shift does to nitrogen

Soil pH acts on the nitrogen cycle in opposite directions for different gases.

**Nitrous oxide falls.** Denitrifying bacteria reduce nitrate step by step to nitric oxide, nitrous oxide and finally inert dinitrogen ($\text{N}_2$). The last step needs the enzyme $\text{N}_2\text{O}$ reductase, which works poorly in acidic soil, so at low pH more of the denitrified nitrogen leaves as $\text{N}_2\text{O}$ rather than $\text{N}_2$[^3]<sup>,</sup>[^6]. Raising pH shifts the end products towards $\text{N}_2$. That matters for climate, because $\text{N}_2\text{O}$ warms about $273$ times as much as $\text{CO}_2$ per unit mass over 100 years[^7].

**Ammonia rises.** Dissolved ammonium and ammonia are in equilibrium, $\text{NH}_4^+ \rightleftharpoons \text{NH}_3 + \text{H}^+$, and only the neutral $\text{NH}_3$ can volatilise. A higher pH moves the balance towards it, so the same pH rise that cuts $\text{N}_2\text{O}$ raises ammonia emission, an air-quality cost.

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
    Basalt["Basalt dissolution: soil pH rises"] --> Denit["Denitrification ends more often at N2"]
    Basalt --> Nit["Nitrification yields less N2O per unit"]
    Basalt --> Eq["NH4+ / NH3 equilibrium shifts towards NH3"]
    Denit --> N2O["Less N2O and NO: climate benefit"]
    Nit --> N2O
    Eq --> NH3["More NH3: air-quality cost"]

    class Basalt indigo
    class N2O sage
    class NH3 rust
    classDef indigo fill:#1d4a62,stroke:#c97d62,stroke-width:1.5px,color:#ffffff
    classDef rust fill:#a04b2d,stroke:#c97d62,stroke-width:1.5px,color:#ffffff
    classDef sage fill:#95a87f,stroke:#3b1a18,stroke-width:1.5px,color:#3b1a18
```

## Simulating it in CLM5

In Val Martin et al.[^4], the weathering chemistry does **not** run inside CLM5. A separate ERW model computes how much soil pH rises after 25 years of annual basalt application, from alkalinity mass and flux balances, for cropland in five regions (North America, Brazil, Europe, India and China) chosen to remove $2\text{ Gt CO}_2\text{ yr}^{-1}$ in total[^5]. Those pH changes are added to CLM5's initial soil pH, and the two models are coupled asynchronously: CLM5 supplies nitrogen fluxes and the starting pH, and the weathering model returns the pH change[^8].

Inside CLM5 the nitrogen scheme was rebuilt so that pH can matter:

| Process | How pH enters |
|---|---|
| Nitrification | the fraction emitted as $\text{N}_2\text{O}$ is $721.86\,e^{-2.387\,\text{pH}}$, which falls as pH rises; at pH $5.8$–$6.2$ it gives $3$–$7 \times 10^{-4}$, close to the old constant of $6 \times 10^{-4}$ |
| Denitrification | pH sets the total nitrogen lost, $0.0016\,e^{1.006\,\text{pH}}$, and the $\text{N}_2:\text{N}_2\text{O}$ ratio of the products, which shifts towards $\text{N}_2$ as pH rises |
| Nitric oxide | from a $\text{NO}:\text{N}_2\text{O}$ ratio set by soil air-filled pore space, so it follows the $\text{N}_2\text{O}$ processes |
| Ammonia | the scheme of Fung et al.[^9] with a pH factor rising from $0.6$ below pH $5$ to $1.0$ above pH $8$ |

For the $\text{N}_2\text{O}$ and $\text{NO}$ processes, soil pH comes from the Harmonized World Soil Database rather than CLM5's default constant of $6.5$. The ammonia scheme keeps a baseline of $6.5$ and adds the weathering pH change on top, because spatially varying pH overestimated ammonia from alkaline soils.

The model was benchmarked against a field trial at the Energy Farm in Illinois, where basalt-treated and untreated plots were compared. It simulated $\text{N}_2\text{O}$ reductions of $21$–$25\%$ for maize and $44\%$ for soybean, against observed reductions of $12$–$32\%$ and $31\%$[^4].

At the scale of the deployment scenario[^4]:

| | $\text{N}_2\text{O}$ | $\text{NO}$ | $\text{NH}_3$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| Five regions, absolute change | $-0.42\text{ Tg N yr}^{-1}$ | $-0.25\text{ Tg N yr}^{-1}$ | $+0.17\text{ Tg N yr}^{-1}$ |
| Five regions, share of agricultural emission | $-19\%$ | $-17\%$ | $+2\%$ |
| Share of the global total | $-13\%$ | $-12\%$ | $+1\%$ |
| North America | $-28\%$ | $-24\%$ | about $+10\%$ on neutral to alkaline soils |
| China | $-16\%$ | $-18\%$ | |
| Europe | $-13\%$ | $-12\%$ | |

<small>From the body text of Val Martin et al.[^4] The paper's abstract rounds both the $\text{N}_2\text{O}$ and $\text{NO}$ reductions to $18\%$.</small>

The paper reports these as emission changes. It does not convert the $\text{N}_2\text{O}$ reduction into a $\text{CO}_2$-equivalent benefit to add to the carbon removed, and it lists its own limitations: the ratio of nitrification to denitrification in CLM5 is probably too low, the ammonia pH function is a first approximation with very few basalt observations behind it, the weathering parameterisation needs more field data, only direct soil fluxes are counted, and the global runs use annual rather than monthly pH changes.

## Key takeaways

- Basalt dissolution turns $\text{CO}_2$ into bicarbonate that rivers carry to the ocean, and the same reaction consumes hydrogen ions, raising soil pH.
- Higher pH lets denitrification run further to $\text{N}_2$ and lowers the $\text{N}_2\text{O}$ yield of nitrification, cutting $\text{N}_2\text{O}$; it also shifts ammonium towards volatile ammonia, raising $\text{NH}_3$.
- In Val Martin et al., a separate weathering model computes the pH change and CLM5 computes the nitrogen response; the two are coupled asynchronously.
- For deployment removing $2\text{ Gt CO}_2\text{ yr}^{-1}$ across five regions, agricultural $\text{N}_2\text{O}$ falls $19\%$ and $\text{NO}$ $17\%$, while $\text{NH}_3$ rises $2\%$. North America changes most.
- The study reports emission changes only; it does not express the $\text{N}_2\text{O}$ reduction as a $\text{CO}_2$-equivalent benefit.
